thesis: Cadillac did not simply glue its badge onto a Chevrolet: it made real, documented changes to the J-car -- standard leather and air conditioning, its own tuned touring suspension, even its own rear axle bushings -- and then asked about 43% more than the most expensive Cavalier sedan for them. The changes were real but narrow, and mostly invisible from the driver's seat, which is why a car the press initially liked ended up as the definitive cautionary tale about badge engineering.
hook: In 1982 Cadillac sold a car with leather seats, a tachometer, alloy wheels and its own specially tuned suspension -- and it is still remembered as one of the worst cars ever made.
open_questions: The central price comparison now rests on d01 (base Cimarron vs base Cavalier CL sedan, ~43%). If a period Chevrolet price list or a readable Curbside Classic page later confirms u01's equipment-matched Cavalier figure, beat b4 should be revisited -- an equipment-matched premium would be the fairer number still, and would likely be smaller than 43%.

c02's named rivals (Volvo GL, Saab 900S, BMW 320i) come from The Drive, but the 1982 dealer brochure read in full for this episode names no competitors at all. Worth locating the specific Cadillac marketing piece The Drive is describing before b2 leans harder on that list.

Nothing in the fact pack evidences WHY Cadillac wanted a compact (x02 is unresolved with zero sources). Beat b2 currently works around this by describing the pitch rather than the motive. A period business-press source on Cadillac's early-1980s demographics would let b2 make the stronger causal argument it currently cannot.

beats.purpose: Open on the contradiction the episode resolves -- a genuinely well-equipped car that history records as a disaster -- and withhold the name to buy curiosity.
beats.summary: Cold open on the tension: a 1982 car with standard leather seating, full instrumentation including a tachometer, alloy wheels and a manufacturer-tuned touring suspension, which nonetheless landed on TIME's 2007 list of the fifty worst cars ever made.
beats.narration_direction: Every factual detail here must come from e01 (leather, tach, alloys) and e03 (tuned touring suspension) -- both are from Cadillac's own brochure, so they are safe. Mark the 'worst cars' judgment as 2007, per l01's forbidden inferences: do NOT imply that was the 1982 verdict. Withhold the model name until the end of the beat. Do not state any price or premium here -- the numbers are earned in b4.

beats.purpose: Establish what Cadillac said it was doing, using its own marketing -- replacing the previously unsourced claim about aging buyers with something actually evidenced.
beats.summary: Cadillac pitched the Cimarron as a deliberate reach for a different customer: its brochure opened with 'a new kind of Cadillac for a new kind of Cadillac owner', and its marketing named the Volvo GL, Saab 900S and BMW 320i as the cars it meant to take on.
beats.narration_direction: AUDIT FIX: this beat previously asserted an aging buyer base and fuel-economy/downsizing pressure with nothing behind them (now x02, unresolved, zero sources). Do NOT reinstate that. The move is to describe Cadillac's PITCH -- which is documented in its own brochure (c01) -- and let the audience infer the motive, rather than asserting a demographic cause we cannot source. Do not name the Audi 4000 or Honda Accord (u03 unresolved). Per c02's conflicting_evidence, attribute the rival list to 'Cadillac's marketing', not to 'the brochure' -- the brochure we actually hold names no rivals.

beats.purpose: Explain the structural fact that constrains everything else -- five divisions, one car -- and the timing pressure Cadillac was under.
beats.summary: The Cimarron was one of five versions of GM's J-body, alongside the Chevrolet Cavalier, Pontiac J2000, Buick Skyhawk and Oldsmobile Firenza, sharing front-wheel drive, MacPherson strut front suspension, a semi-independent rear and rack and pinion steering. Cadillac came to the program late -- by one account about eleven months before launch -- and GM president Pete Estes reportedly warned Cadillac's general manager that there wasn't time to turn the J-car into a Cadillac.
beats.narration_direction: Use 'reportedly' on the Estes remark (t01 requires the hedge -- the underlying citation was never retrieved) and 'by one account' on the eleven-month timeline (t02 was only ever a search snippet). The architecture list (a01) comes from the brochure's own cutaway callouts, so it can be stated plainly. Keep the shared-architecture point and the Cadillac-changes point separate -- the latter is b4's job -- so the audience gets the constraint before the response to it.

beats.purpose: Deliver the episode's factual core and correct both popular distortions at once: that Cadillac changed nothing, and that the car cost double a Cavalier.
beats.summary: Cadillac's changes were real and documented in its own brochure: air conditioning, leather seating, a leather-wrapped wheel, full instrumentation with a tachometer, alloy wheels and deep-pile carpeting all standard, an acoustical insulation package, an exclusively tuned touring suspension and even Cadillac-specific rear axle arm bushings. But most of that could be optioned onto its GM siblings, and the price gap was large: about 43% over the top-trim Cavalier CL sedan, or about 83% over the cheapest stripped Cadet coupe -- the comparison that produces the familiar 'nearly double' line.
beats.narration_direction: The single most important beat for numerical discipline. Lead the price comparison with d01 (~43% vs the top Cavalier sedan) as the headline figure; introduce d02 (~83%) only with its comparator explicitly named as the cheapest stripped Cadet coupe, and use it to explain where the widespread 'nearly double' claim comes from rather than repeating it unqualified. Both d01 and d02 forbid unattributed use. Do NOT air any equipment-matched Cavalier price or the ~25% figure (u01/u02 unresolved). Pair e01-e04 with x01 in the same breath -- Cadillac made these things standard, but standard is not exclusive; that tension IS the beat. Attribute the equipment and suspension details to Cadillac's own brochure on screen, since that is where they come from.

beats.purpose: Correct the retrospective distortion: separate what the press said in 1981-82 from the reputation that formed decades later.
beats.summary: Contemporary reception was split rather than uniformly hostile. Road & Track timed the 1.8-litre car at 15.9 seconds to 60 mph and called it painfully slow. Car and Driver's original August 1981 test, by Rich Ceppos, was favorable -- the magazine's own later reprint carries the standfirst 'It's an embarrassment now, but we didn't think so then', and Ceppos later said he was embarrassed at how warmly he had received the car.
beats.narration_direction: Hold three time layers apart: the 1981-82 reviews (r01, r02), the reviewer's later regret (r03, explicitly retrospective), and the reputation in b7. Do NOT quote 'one of the boldest moves ever made by a car company' -- q01 is unresolved and its forbidden inferences also rule out loose paraphrase. The C&D standfirst in r02's safe_wording IS quotable and does the same narrative work. Per r01, do not extend the performance criticism to the later V6 cars.

beats.purpose: Show sustained effort without recovery, using only the volume statement the sources actually agree on.
beats.summary: Cadillac kept working on the car: a 2.8-litre V6 arrived as an option in 1985 and was standard by 1987. It did not turn the model around. By its final year, 1988, Cadillac was moving only around six thousand of them, and production ended after that model year.
beats.narration_direction: AUDIT FIX: this beat previously asserted a 1983 2.0-litre engine and Bilstein/touring suspension upgrades with no supporting claim (now x03, unresolved). Do not reinstate them -- m01's V6 carries the 'they kept trying' point on its own. Do NOT read out a year-by-year sales table: s01 and s02 are two irreconcilable series and s02 is explicitly not airable. Use only s04, the roughly-six-thousand final year, which all three independent sources agree on in shape, and say 'around six thousand' rather than 6,454, since the sources differ by about 10%. Avoid 'collapsed' and similar intensifiers -- the numerical claim rule requires a derived claim for that kind of characterisation and none exists.

beats.purpose: Land the thesis by naming what the car actually became -- a reference point -- and make clear that this status was assigned in hindsight.
beats.summary: The Cimarron's real afterlife is as a case study. TIME named it to its fifty worst cars list in 2007, twenty-five years after launch, and a former Cadillac product director is said to have kept a photo of one in his office as a reminder. The verdict that defines the car was reached long after anyone stopped buying it.
beats.narration_direction: Date the TIME judgment explicitly to 2007 and set it against b5's contemporary reception -- the gap between the two is the closing argument. Use 'is said to have' on the Howell anecdote (l02 requires the hedge and forbids generalising one person's habit into company policy). Close on the thesis: the changes were real but narrow, and the reputation was retrospective.
